questions.knowledge_point: Computing Mass or Charge Over a Rectangular Domain
questions.problem: The mass density function $\lambda $ of a rectangular flat plate that occupies the region $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2}$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=y{e}^{xy}.$ What is the total mass of the plate?
questions.worked_solution:
The mass $M$ of a plate that occupies the region $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2}$ with mass density $\lambda (x,y)=y{e}^{xy}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:      

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y[{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{e}^{xy}]_{0}^{1}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({e}^{y}-{e}^{0})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({e}^{y}-1)\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}({e}^{y}-1)\,\text{d}y & =[{e}^{y}-y]_{0}^{2} \\  & =({e}^{2}-2)-(1-0) \\  & ={e}^{2}-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the mass of the plate is $M={e}^{2}-3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing Mass or Charge Over a Rectangular Domain
questions.problem: The mass density function $\lambda $ of a rectangular wooden flat plate that occupies the region $D={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1}$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=6{x}^{2}y.$ What is the total mass of the plate?
questions.worked_solution:
The mass $M$ of a plate that occupies the region $D={(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1}$ with mass density $\lambda (x,y)=6{x}^{2}y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}6{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:      

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}6{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{-2}^{2}6{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{-2}^{2}6{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6y[{\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6y{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{-2}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6y(\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-2)^{2}}{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}32y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}32y\,\text{d}y & =[16{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =16\cdot ({1}^{2}-0) \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the mass of the plate is $M=16.$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing Mass or Charge Over a Rectangular Domain
questions.problem: Find the total charge $Q$ of a metal plate that occupies the region $D={(x,y):0\le x\le \pi ,\,0\le y\le 1}$ with charge density $\rho (x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).$
questions.worked_solution:
The total charge $Q$ of a plate that occupies the region $D={(x,y):0\le x\le \pi ,\,0\le y\le 1}$ with charge density $\rho (x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & ={∬}_{D}y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:

$$
{∬}_{D}y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y{[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)}{y}]}_{0}^{\pi }\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)]_{0}^{\pi }\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)-\operatorname{sin}⁡0]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)\,\text{d}y & ={[-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)}{\pi }]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)}{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 0)}{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }+\frac{1}{\pi } \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the charge of the plate is $Q=\frac{2}{\pi }.$

questions.problem: The mass density function $\lambda $ of a rectangular flat plate that occupies the region $D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2}$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}.$ What is the total mass of the plate?
questions.worked_solution:
The mass $M$ of a plate that occupies the region $D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2}$ with mass density $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:      

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}{[-\frac{1}{x}]}_{1}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}(-\frac{1}{2}-(-1))\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\,\text{d}y & ={[\frac{{y}^{3}}{6}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{3}}{6}-0 \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the mass of the plate is $M=\frac{4}{3}.$

questions.problem: The mass density function $\lambda $ of a rectangular iron flat plate that occupies the region $D={(x,y)\,:\,{e}^{2}\le x\le {e}^{6},\,0\le y\le 3}$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{{y}^{3}}{x}.$ What is the total mass of the plate?
questions.worked_solution:
The mass $M$ of a plate that occupies the region $D={(x,y)\,:\,{e}^{2}\le x\le {e}^{6},\,0\le y\le 3}$ with mass density $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{{y}^{3}}{x}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\frac{{y}^{3}}{x}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:      

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{y}^{3}}{x}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{{e}^{2}}^{{e}^{6}}\frac{{y}^{3}}{x}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{{e}^{2}}^{{e}^{6}}\frac{{y}^{3}}{x}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{3}[{\int }_{{e}^{2}}^{{e}^{6}}\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{3}[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]_{{e}^{2}}^{{e}^{6}}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{6}-\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y & =[{y}^{4}]_{0}^{3} \\  & ={3}^{4}-(0)^{4} \\  & =81\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the mass of the plate is $M=81.$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing Mass or Charge Over a Type I or Type II Region
questions.problem: Find the total charge $Q$ of the lower half of the circular disk ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9$ with charge density function $\rho $ given by $\rho (x,y)=y$
questions.worked_solution:
The total charge $Q$ of  the lower half of the circular disk  $D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9,\,y\le 0}$ with charge density $\rho (x,y)=y$ is given by

$$
Q={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A.
$$

Since $y\le 0,$ we obtain

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9\,⟹\,y\ge -\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}.
$$

Let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/af77552bd144fb70dfe8787060c0136f54955d20cdd2543391bd040b01a460d2.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- We already know the intersection of the circle with the line $y=0.$ So, the $x$-limits are $-3\le x\le 3.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/32db7009737aa47c8b5a96da91d72b0db95530271f463a9f7d35f715793cbea8.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region:

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-3\le x\le 3,\,-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}\le y\le 0}
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A={\int }_{-3}^{3}{\int }_{-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}^{0}y\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & ={\int }_{-3}^{3}[{\int }_{-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}^{0}y\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{3}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}^{0}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{3}(0-\frac{9-{x}^{2}}{2})\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-3}^{3}({x}^{2}-9)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-3}^{3}({x}^{2}-9)\,dx & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-9x]}_{-3}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[(9-27)-(-9+27)] \\  & =-18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total charge of the lower half of the circular disk is $Q=-18.$

questions.problem: A metal plate occupies the region $D={(x,y):-1\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le {y}^{2}}.$ The charge density of the plate is given by $\rho (x,y)=x{y}^{2}.$ Find the total charge $Q$ of the plate.
questions.worked_solution:
The total charge $Q$ of a plate that occupies the region $D$ with charge density $\rho (x,y)=x{y}^{2}$ is given by

$$
Q={∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.
$$

Let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/1cbe96aa4bf517302a2329db9f8eb2e9c56873e4d5a18cd5f1cd676543e97086.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type II region. So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{2}(\frac{{y}^{4}}{2}-0)\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{6}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{y}^{6}\,\text{d}y & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{{y}^{7}}{7}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{{1}^{7}}{7}-(-\frac{{1}^{7}}{7})) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total charge of the plate is $Q=\frac{1}{7}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing Mass or Charge Over a Type I or Type II Region
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/c497efbb28bade962b997d7e14f5a272f0cead56f7567b1baaebae695c7c80f4.png)

An iron flat plate occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the curves $x=0,y=e,$ and $y={e}^{x},$ as shown above. The mass density function $\lambda $ of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{1}{y}.$ Find the total mass of the plate.
questions.worked_solution:
The mass of the plate occupying the region $D$ with mass density $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{1}{y}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $D$ is a type I region. 

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & =e \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So the $x$-limits are $0\le x\le 1.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/95a6d9b0bc464c719311dc900967ebd06a3aa3d3004cfe5303359eecb20551e7.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,{e}^{x}\le y\le e}.
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{e}^{x}}^{e}\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{e}^{x}}^{e}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[\operatorname{ln}⁡y]_{{e}^{x}}^{e}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1-x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-x)\,\text{d}x & ={[x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1-\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total mass of the iron plate is $M=\frac{1}{2}.$

A thin sheet of caramel occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the curves $x=1,y=x$ and $y=2,$ as shown above. The mass density function $\lambda $ of the sheet is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{y}{x}.$ Find the total mass of the caramel sheet.
questions.worked_solution:
The mass of the caramel sheet occupying the region $D$ with mass density $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{y}{x}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $D$ is a type I region. 

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

- To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So the $x$-limits are $1\le x\le 2.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/281ea7be1ef48c149bb4bcfd09aa41357caa8bb28adfc48285d298fb3cf89f3c.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D={(x,y):1\le x\le 2,\,x\le y\le 2}.
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x}^{2}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{x}^{2}\frac{y}{x}\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{x}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{x}[\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{x}-\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{x}-\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{{2}^{2}}{4})-(2\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\frac{{1}^{2}}{4}) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total mass of the ice sheet is $M=2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{3}{4}.$

questions.problem: A metal plate occupies the region $D={(x,y):0\le x\le \sqrt{\pi },\,0\le y\le \operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2}}.$ The charge density of the plate is given by $\rho (x,y)=x.$ Find the total charge $Q$ of the plate.
questions.worked_solution:
The total charge $Q$ of a plate that occupies the region $D$ with charge density $\rho (x,y)=x$ is given by

$$
Q={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A.
$$

Let's sketch our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/2b179e35ae9af5a13d43c9a64bee99ee4ed87c257b623184f9165e14c24f3dee.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type I region. So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2}}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2}}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}[{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y]x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}[y]_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2}}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}x\operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }}x\operatorname{sin}⁡{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi }} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total charge of the plate is $Q=1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing Mass or Charge Using Polar Coordinates
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/7583a2da0bff7d66a3512c58f67692100af403b61b19a9b52347519b30823342.png)

Find the total charge $Q$ of a metal plate that occupies the region $D$ enclosed between  the parts of  the curves ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ and ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ as shown above, and has charge density $\rho (x,y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the region $D$ represents a half-annulus enclosed between the circles of the radiuses $1$ and $2$ centered at the origin.

The total charge $Q$ of an object occupying the region $D$ with charge density $\rho (x,y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}$ is given by

$$
Q={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}\rho (x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }\rho (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

The following equations connect Cartesian and polar coordinates:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ we obtain $r=2.$

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ we obtain $r=1.$

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}[r]_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(2-1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[\theta ]_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\, \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-(-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total charge of the object is $Q=\pi .$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/514a3cd39f24a7b2477e6214964d69cd743a26645eba7f4b797af832b565fa93.png)

An object occupies the region $D$ in the second quadrant enclosed between the curves ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$, as shown above. The mass density function $\lambda $ of the object is given by $\lambda (x,y)=y.$ Find the mass of the object.
questions.worked_solution:
The mass of an object which occupies the region $D$ with mass density $\lambda (x,y)=y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We will convert this to polar coordinates using the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }\lambda (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion between the disks of radii $1$ and $3$ centered at the origin. 

The following equations connect cartesian and polar coordinates:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ we obtain $r=1.$

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ we obtain $r=3.$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ The entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $\theta =\pi ,$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/7f3b2717946956ade07c252413130a730070e370cab85c73d866fa9506604106.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 3,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Finally, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (9-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{26}{3}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{26}{3}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{26}{3}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{26}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total mass of the object is $M=\frac{26}{3}.$

questions.problem: Find the mass of an ice object which has the form of a quarter-disk, in the fourth quadrant, of radius $3$ centered at the origin and mass density function $\lambda $ given by $\lambda (x,y)=8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$
questions.worked_solution:
The mass of a quarter-disk $D$ of radius $3$ centered at the origin with mass density $\lambda (x,y)=8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }\lambda (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/4f7b1647d893512605ee1a2e9cee3e5511a00dc7ad9b1765fff1d0ba0710895f.png)

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0}.
$$

Finally, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}8({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{3}8{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(81-0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =162{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =162[\theta ]_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =162(0-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =81\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total mass of the quarter-disk is $M=81\pi .$

questions.problem: Find the mass of a glass object which has the form of an upper half-disk of radius $3$ centered at the origin and mass density function $\lambda $ given by $\lambda (x,y)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The mass of an upper half-disk $D$ of radius $3$ centered at the origin with mass density $\lambda (x,y)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }\lambda (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/d8e2f73ce8840471143689748e188debaf5fde8f3aaf5021fd8d99c4f86a72d6.png)

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Finally, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\frac{81}{4}-0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{4}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{81}{4}(-(-1)+1) \\  & =\frac{81}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total mass of the upper half-disk is $M=\frac{81}{2}.$

questions.problem: Find the mass of a plastic object which has the form of a lower half-disk of radius $4$ centered at the origin and mass density function $\lambda $ given by $\lambda (x,y)={y}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The mass of a lower half-disk $D$ of radius $4$ centered at the origin with mass density $\lambda (x,y)=y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\text{ }\text{d}A={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }\lambda (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/379073190f15a5e80c696b8f5bb77132dd515ca2493b8f0407354bbac923bb91.png)

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Finally, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta [\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (64-0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =64{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32[\theta -\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{2}]_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =32\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total mass of the upper half-disk is $M=32\pi .$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing Mass or Charge Over a Rectangular Domain
canonical_examples.problem: Find the total charge $Q$ of a metal plate that occupies the region $D = \{ (x,y) : 0 \le x \le 1, \, 0 \le y \le 2\}$ with charge density $\rho (x,y) = 4 - 3y^2 + 2x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The total charge $Q$ of a plate that occupies the region $D = \{ (x,y) : 0 \leq x \leq 1, \, 0 \leq y \leq 2\}$ with charge density $\rho (x,y) = 4 - 3y^2 + 2x$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & ={∬}_{D}(4-3{y}^{2}+2x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:

$$
\iint\limits_{D} (4 - 3y^2 + 2x) \:\textrm{d}A
= \int_{0}^2 \left[ \int_{0}^1 (4 - 3y^2 + 2x) \:\textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}y
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(4-3{y}^{2}+2x)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[4x-3{y}^{2}x+{x}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[(4(1)-3{y}^{2}(1)+(1)^{2})-(4(0)-3{y}^{2}(0)-(0)^{2})]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(5-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}(5-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y & =[5y-{y}^{3}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =(5(2)-(2)^{3})-(5(0)-(0)^{3}) \\  & =(10-8)-0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the charge of the plate is $Q=2.$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066271/assets/f0db928874dba8d872cde46d1467686010f3484765b2d7e39807b5a32a131b09.png)

Find the total charge $Q$ of a copper plate that occupies the region $D$ shown above, and has charge density 

$$
\rho (x,y) = \dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}  .
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that the region $D$ represents one-quarter of the disk of radius $3$ centered at 
$\left(0,0\right).$

The total charge $Q$ of an object occupying the region $D$ with charge density $\rho (x,y) =  \dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}$ is given by

$$
Q = \iint\limits_{D} \dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}  \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \rho(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ \rho(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

The following equations connect Cartesian and polar coordinates:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the curve $x^2+y^2=9$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =9 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =9 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =9 \\ {r}^{2} & =9 \\ r & =3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 3, \: \pi \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{4x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\sqrt{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [{\int }_{0}^{3}r\,\text{d}r]\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (\frac{9}{2}-0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =18{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =18[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =18[-1-0] \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total charge of the quarter-disk is $Q = - 18.$
